message.reasoning:
I need to write a JUnit 4 test for PosixParser (Cli-2b), using commons-lang-2.1.jar and junit-3.8.1.jar on the classpath even though the test itself should use JUnit 4 annotations like org.junit.Test, per the task requirements.

I'll study the Options and Option classes -- their hasOption, getOption, hasArg, and hasArgs methods -- to write test cases matching real parser behavior. Since flatten is a protected method on Parser (which PosixParser extends), my test class needs to live in the org.apache.commons.cli package to call it directly rather than using reflection.

I'm planning several flatten() test cases covering "--" long options, "--opt=value" syntax, single hyphen "-", and short option "-a" where the option exists, using Options built with addOption and OptionBuilder.

Now I'm mapping out more scenarios: short option "-x" that doesn't exist with stopAtNonOption true or false, multi-character tokens matching hasOption directly, and burstToken behavior when bursting a token into individual option characters -- including a known Cli-2b defect where the hasArgs() branch in process() is actually unreachable dead code since the outer hasArg() check already filters it out.

I'm also tracing through non-option token handling in process() depending on whether currentOption is null and stopAtNonOption's effect, plus how gobble() dumps remaining tokens once eatTheRest is triggered.

Then I'm mapping out the API surface for the older commons-cli Options and Option classes — addOption variants, hasOption, getOption, and hasArg/hasArgs behavior based on numberOfArgs — to figure out what constructors and setters I'll need for building test fixtures.

I realize the setArgs/UNLIMITED_VALUES path is actually dead code given the outer hasArg() check, so I'll skip it and focus on the branches that are actually reachable.

I'm placing my test class in the same package as PosixParser so I can call the protected flatten and burstToken methods directly, since protected access extends to same-package classes even without subclassing. Testing burstToken directly would require setting up private instance fields first, so it may be simpler to exercise it indirectly through flatten.

I'm sketching out test cases: verifying "--foo=bar" splits into ["--foo","bar"], "--foo" alone stays as a single token, a lone "-" stays as-is, and I'm starting to design a case involving a defined short option.

For validating currentOption state, I realize non-option values only pass through process() when stopAtNonOption is true, so I need that flag set to actually exercise those branches. I'm now planning a test where an undefined short option triggers stopAtNonOption behavior with trailing arguments.

Right, this matches standard Commons CLI behavior where hasOption strips leading hyphens before checking shortOpts/longOpts, so it's well-known library behavior rather than an assumption I'm guessing at. With only option "a" defined, checking "-x" strips to "x" and finds no match.

For test 6 with stopAtNonOption false, the "-x" token gets ignored, then "rest1" and "rest2" get added normally as they're not recognized as options—so tokens end up the same as test 5, just via a different code path. Now I'm moving on to check the next test case involving token length.

For length-3 tokens like "-ab" that match a registered multi-character option exactly, the token should be added whole without bursting into individual characters. Then for burstToken behavior, when a character in the middle of a token matches an option that takes an argument, the remaining substring should be captured as that option's argument value.

For test 9, I'm working through the case where all burst characters correspond to boolean flags with no arguments, so each gets added as its own separate "-x" token in sequence. Test 10 sets up the case where stopAtNonOption is true and a character doesn't correspond to any known option, which should trigger reprocessing of the remaining substring as a fresh token.

After gobble(), remaining tokens get appended directly, so with input like {"-ax", "extra"} the expected final result would be ["-a","--","x","extra"]. For test 11, I'm checking the case where stopAtNonOption is false, meaning burstToken adds "-x" directly without calling process, using the same 'a' registered/'x' unregistered setup as before.

Then for test 12, when there's no preceding option and a non-option token arrives with stopAtNonOption true, the else branch fires: eatTheRest becomes true, and tokens get "--" followed by the value, so {"value1"} alone should yield ["--","value1"].

For test 13, I'm setting up {"-a", "value1"} where option 'a' has hasArg=true and stopAtNonOption=true - processing "-a" sets currentOption and adds it to tokens, then processing "value1" hits the true branch since currentOption is set with hasArg true, so it just adds the value and clears currentOption, giving expected tokens ["-a","value1"].

Now I need to check test 14 where stopAtNonOption is false - in that case a non-option token just gets added directly to tokens regardless of currentOption state, so {"value1"} with stopAtNonOption=false simply yields ["value1"].

I should also cover edge cases: an empty arguments array should produce an empty tokens array, and I want to verify what happens when Options is null but the tokens don't actually need to consult it (e.g. plain strings or "--"), confirming options are only touched when actually necessary. I'm also planning a helper method to build Options objects with addOption(opt, hasArg, description) for these test setups.

For boundary testing, I want to cover a lone "--" token which should just get added literally as "--", and a "--foo=" token with a trailing empty value that should split into "--foo" and an empty string. I should also consider testing "--=value" where the equals sign appears right after the double hyphen.

I'm also noting that the inner branch checking hasArgs() inside process() is dead code since the outer condition already requires hasArg() true — this matches the known Cli-2b defect, worth flagging in my summary even though it won't show up in coverage.

Now I'm finalizing the test file with the necessary imports for JUnit assertions, Arrays, and the Commons-CLI Options, Option, and PosixParser classes.

Given the constraint about only having commons-lang-2.1.jar and junit-3.8.1.jar available, there's a conflict since JUnit 4 annotations wouldn't normally be present—but since the task explicitly asks for a JUnit4-style test class named PosixParserTest, I'll proceed with standard org.junit imports as instructed and set aside that classpath concern. I'll also make sure the package declaration matches org.apache.commons.cli so the test can access package-private members.

I'm planning a setUp method that creates a fresh PosixParser and Options instance before each test, and since the test lives in the same package, I can call the protected flatten method directly on the parser. I'll write assertions using assertArrayEquals to compare expected and actual token arrays, covering edge cases like a lone "-" token and an empty string argument, then assemble the complete test file.
